Burleigh County at a glance

Burleigh County lies in the middle of southern North Dakota, with Bismarck as seat and largest city. About 98,458 people lived here at the 2020 count, and households earn a median $88,701. One bill folds together county, city or township, school and smaller districts. A seller's first step is learning which district the parcel is in.

Mill levies by taxing district

Every parcel falls in a taxing district that pairs a city or township with a school district, and each pairing has its own total mill levy. A mill is one thousandth of a dollar of taxable value. The county's 2025 levy sheet gives these totals for a sample of districts:

  • City of Bismarck: 237.10 mills
  • City of Lincoln: 227.55
  • City of Wing: 204.52
  • City of Regan: 272.08
  • South Wilton: 274.74
  • Menoken (rural district): 109.40
  • Canfield (rural, three listings): 194.61, 153.92 and 153.92

Rural parcels outside any city usually carry lower totals because there is no city levy. Some townships appear more than once on the sheet because they straddle more than one school or fire district. Levy sheets for 2022 through 2025 are posted on the county's taxes and levies page.

The county prepares, collects and distributes the tax, but the County Commission has no say over what cities, townships, schools and other districts levy. Each of those bodies sends its budget to the county auditor by October 10. The levy is simply the money the district needs divided by its taxable valuation.

Who values your property

Valuation of real estate countywide is overseen by the Tax Equalization Office, 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck. Write to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506, or call (701) 222-6693 or (701) 222-6691.

The office works under North Dakota Century Code chapter 11-10.1 and relies on computer assisted mass appraisal software. Records are refreshed through reappraisal, building permits and review of sales. Once the State Board of Equalization signs off, the office sends certified values to the auditor, who computes the tax. The State Tax Commissioner then runs a sales ratio study to confirm values track the market.

Local assessors do the first valuation. You can look up property outside Bismarck city limits at burleigh.northdakotaassessors.com, and city property on the City of Bismarck's property information page. The yearly timeline looks like this:

  • February 1: the local assessor sets values
  • April: the local board of equalization reviews them
  • June: the county board reviews what the local boards recommend
  • August: the State Board of Equalization reviews the county boards' work
  • October 10: each taxing body sends its budget to the county auditor

Due dates and penalties

The bill splits into two halves. The first is due March 1 and the second October 15. If you settle the entire amount by February 15, specials included, the consolidated tax drops by 5 percent. Statements go out each December, no later than December 26 under state law, and mobile home bills follow in January.

DatePenalty on first installment and specialsPenalty on second installment
March 23%n/a
May 16%n/a
July 19%n/a
October 15 or 1612% (Oct. 15)6% (Oct. 16)

Mobile homes run on their own calendar. The first installment is due February 28, and 2 percent penalties start March 1, climbing 2 points on the first of each month through June. The second installment is due June 30, with penalties from July 1 through October. The February 15 discount applies to mobile home tax too.

To get the discount or avoid a penalty, your payment has to arrive or carry a postmark on or before the deadline. The county cannot vouch for USPS or courier delivery times. It guarantees a date stamp only for the drop box or for a payment handed over at the Auditor's Office.

Ways to pay your bill

Three channels work: web, phone and postal mail. The web portal is the county's property search, where you enter an address (fewer characters match better) or the parcel number from your statement. Owner names shown there come from the latest statement.

  • Online, or by phone at 1-800-272-9829 with jurisdiction code 4434. Phone payment needs your property number.
  • E-check costs $3.98 for amounts under $10,000 and $19.92 for $10,000 or more.
  • Credit card works online or by phone only, with a 3.61 percent fee and a $1.52 minimum.
  • By mail to Burleigh County Auditor, PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506.

No statement in the mail? Ring the county treasurer at 701-222-6718. A lost statement does not push the deadline back, so request a copy right away.

How to appeal your assessment

You have two paths. One is informal, through the boards of equalization. The other is formal, by requesting an abatement.

Outside Bismarck, the township or city board of equalization hears first-level complaints in April. Inside the city, begin with the city assessor. Before the spring cycle opens, phone the Tax Equalization Office at (701) 222-6693 to learn the meeting dates.

The abatement route is governed by N.D.C.C. 57-23-04. The application goes to the county auditor no later than November 1 of the year following delinquency, and the county commissioners may then cancel or refund some or all of the tax. The form is linked on the Tax Equalization page.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Burleigh County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to delinquent property?

Once taxes, specials and penalties sit unpaid into a third year, the parcel can be taken through tax lien foreclosure. The Auditor/Treasurer follows each such parcel, sends notices to anyone with an interest and runs one sale a year. The county website carries the delinquent list and the sale terms.

  • Ahead of June 1, owners and occupants receive a foreclosure notice.
  • Ahead of August 1, the county newspaper runs a published notice.
  • October 1 is the foreclosure date, with full payment due by 5 p.m.
  • The sale notice goes up in the office and online at least 15 days early.
  • The sale itself falls on the third Tuesday of November.

From October 2 until the sale opens, an owner can still catch up by paying every tax, special, interest charge and penalty. If you want to know what happens to a parcel afterward, read the posted terms or ask the treasurer.

Homestead credit and other exemptions

The Tax Equalization page lists several exemptions. They cover permanent wheelchair confinement, blindness, and paraplegic disabled veteran owners with VA adaptive housing. There is also a farm residence exemption, and a separate application for new or expanding businesses.

Two credits matter to many owners. The homestead credit is for people 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, with income under $70,000. The disabled veteran credit needs an honorable discharge and a VA rating of 50 percent or more.

Filing dates for these credits change from year to year. Call the Tax Equalization Office for the current deadline before relying on any date you find online.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company settles current and back taxes from your sale proceeds. Request a payoff from the county auditor that runs through the actual closing day, since penalty steps on March 2, May 1, July 1 and October 15 move the total.

Special assessments need their own check. If the house is in a city, the city takes those payments and can give you the remaining balance. For rural property, special assessments are paid at the county Auditor/Treasurer's office.

A short checklist before you set a closing date:

  • Auditor's payoff figure, dated for closing day
  • Special assessment balance from the city or county
  • Mortgage payoff letter from your lender
  • Proof of whether this year's installment is paid

We buy Burleigh County houses as-is, including ones with back taxes, so you do not have to catch up the bill before you sell.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Burleigh County treasurer's office?

Visit 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck, ND 58501, or call 701-222-6718. Mail goes to PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506.

How is a Burleigh County tax bill calculated?

Start with half of market value to get assessed value. Residential taxable value is 9 percent of that, and commercial or farm property uses 10 percent. Multiply taxable value by the combined mills of your districts.

When is the Burleigh County tax sale?

It happens on the third Tuesday of November and covers parcels that reached the October 1 foreclosure date. Paying everything owed before the sale opens still stops it.

How do I get the 5 percent discount in Burleigh County?

Pay the entire tax, special assessments included, by February 15. Payments received or postmarked after that date get no discount.

Who do I call to dispute my value?

Phone the Tax Equalization Office at (701) 222-6693 or your city or township assessor. A formal challenge means an abatement application to the auditor, due each November 1 for the prior year's delinquent tax.

Morton County, ND Property Tax Guide: Offices, Appeals and Selling With Tax Due

Cash Home Buyers in North Dakota
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Selling in Morton County? Get a Cash Offer

Morton County in brief

Mandan is both the seat and the biggest city of Morton County, which reaches along the Missouri River in south-central North Dakota. About 33,291 people lived here in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 34,601. Bismarck and Burleigh County lie across the river as part of the same metro area. The tax offices are in Mandan, so a seller near the river should check which side the parcel is on before looking anything up.

Who values property in the county

Valuation is split between two offices. Unincorporated land, plus any city or township that contracts with the county, goes through the county Tax Equalization Office. Inside Mandan, the city's own Assessing and Building Inspections departments do the work.

Market value as of February 1 each year drives residential and commercial assessments. Farmland uses the state's agricultural valuation guide instead. Ten zones cover the county, which means each property is reassessed at least once a decade. When your zone comes up, you get a letter offering either an assessor appointment or a property detail sheet to complete.

Permits follow a similar split. The county Building Inspector covers unincorporated areas, plus Almont and Glen Ullin on request. Flasher, Hebron and New Salem each issue their own.

Credits that can lower a bill

Three programs reduce residential tax in Morton County, and each depends on the owner's situation.

  • Homestead Property Tax Credit: owners 65 or older, or disabled, whose household income stays at or under $70,000 after medical deductions
  • Disabled veteran property tax credit: a disability rating of 50 percent or more
  • Primary Residence Credit, run by the State Tax Commissioner

The Tax Equalization Office also provides a property tax calculator and a farm residence exemption page. If you plan to sell, mention a credit you currently claim, since the buyer will not carry it over automatically.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Morton County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

The treasurer and due dates

Go to 210 2nd Ave NW, Mandan, ND 58554, or call 701-667-3310 to reach the Morton County Treasurer. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., holidays excepted. This elected office, with a four-year term, collects real estate and mobile home tax, mails statements and delinquent notices, and gives lenders the numbers for escrow accounts.

The bill is due January 1 and costs nothing extra through March 1. Settle the full year by February 15 and it falls by 5 percent. Here is the calendar:

DateEvent
February 1Valuation date
AprilCity or township board of equalization
Early JuneCounty board of equalization
AugustState board of equalization
By December 26Statements mailed
February 155% discount deadline
March 1First installment due
October 15Second installment due

Late charges come from section 57-20-01 of the Century Code. They start at 3 percent after March 1 and grow by 3 percent on May 1, July 1 and October 15. A second installment left past October 15 costs 6 percent.

How to appeal your assessment

Phone the assessor right away and ask for a review. Many questions end there without a hearing. The assessment letter shows each property's proposed true and full value, so compare it with what similar homes nearby have sold for.

If a call does not fix it, go to the local equalization meetings, which deal with the current year's value. Cities and townships meet in April, the Morton County Board of Equalization in early June, and the State Board of Equalization finishes its review in August. The state board can lower a value only for owners who appeared at both the local and county boards.

An abatement request is another option. It can cover the current and previous years, the deadline is November 1, and the applicant carries the burden of proof. Call the office to confirm which year applies. Forms come from the State Tax Commissioner's site or the county.

What happens to delinquent property?

A parcel whose taxes, specials and interest remain unpaid in the third year can go to tax lien foreclosure. The county auditor follows each one, sends word to interested parties and holds one sale every year.

  • Before June 1: a foreclosure notice goes to the owner, occupants and others with an interest.
  • Before August 1: a notice of delinquent property is published in the official county newspaper.
  • October 1, 5 p.m.: everything owed must be paid to the County Treasurer.
  • After October 1: the owner can still pay in full before the sale starts.
  • Third Tuesday of November: the annual sale.

The sale itself is announced at least 15 days early in the auditor's office and on the county website, and at least 10 days early in the county newspaper.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Morton County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

You can sell and pay the tax out of the proceeds, and a cash buyer can often close faster than a lender-financed buyer. The title company asks the Treasurer for the payoff and pays it at closing.

The delinquency calendar is the reason to move early. After a county takes a tax deed, an owner can buy the property back only before it is resold, either in full or under an installment contract with at least 25 percent paid in cash. A tax foreclosure can also wipe out a mortgage, because the tax lien comes first.

Before you set a closing date:

  • Call the Treasurer at 701-667-3310 for a payoff that covers the whole year.
  • Find out whether any credit you claim ends with the sale.
  • Check the delinquency calendar to see how close the parcel is to October 1.
  • Tell the title company whether the house is inside Mandan or in the county, so the right assessor is contacted.

We buy Morton County houses as they are, including homes in Mandan and the smaller towns, and we work with your title company on the county payoff.

What to bring when you call

Whether you phone the Treasurer, the Tax Equalization Office or the City of Mandan, the first question will be which parcel you mean. Have the address and the parcel number from your latest statement in front of you. If you inherited the property, have the estate paperwork handy, because the person on the phone may need to confirm who is allowed to receive information.

Write down the answers as you go. For the Treasurer, you want the amount owed for the whole year and the date the figure runs through. For the assessor, you want the proposed true and full value and the zone the property is in. For a lender, you want the escrow balance, since the treasurer's office supplies figures to lenders for those accounts.

How a cash sale compares

A lender-financed buyer needs an appraisal and loan approval, and either can slow the closing. A cash buyer skips both, which helps when the delinquency calendar is close or you need to be out of the house by a certain date.

The county still gets paid in full at closing in either case. The difference is who else has to say yes before the deed changes hands. With a cash purchase there is no loan underwriter in the middle, and no repair negotiation after an inspection, because the buyer prices the condition into the offer from the start.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Morton County?

The Morton County Treasurer, at 210 2nd Ave NW in Mandan. The phone is 701-667-3310.

Does Mandan assess its own property?

Yes. Mandan runs its own assessing and building inspection departments inside city limits. The county assesses unincorporated areas and towns that contract with it.

When is Morton County property tax due?

The tax is due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1. A full payment by February 15 earns 5 percent off, and the second installment date is October 15.

When does Morton County foreclose tax liens?

The foreclosure date is October 1 at 5 p.m. The annual sale of delinquent property is the third Tuesday of November.

Which credits can reduce a Morton County bill?

The Homestead Credit, the disabled veteran credit and the Primary Residence Credit. The homestead income limit is $70,000 after medical deductions.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Ward County?

Ward County at a glance

Minot is both the seat and the largest city of Ward County, in north-central North Dakota. The 2020 census put the county at 69,919 people, fourth in the state. Berthold, Burlington, Carpio, Des Lacs, Donnybrook, Douglas, Kenmare, Makoti, Ryder, Sawyer and Surrey are the other incorporated cities, and farmland covers most of the ground outside them.

Minot Air Force Base employs the most people in the county, an estimated 6,957 on base, and more than 11,000 are tied to it once families and civilian staff are counted. Because service members relocate on orders, a base-connected seller often needs a closing date to plan around.

How a Ward County house is taxed

Take the true and full value of the house and keep 4.5 percent of it: that is the taxable value. Multiply it by the combined mill levy of every district taxing the parcel. One mill equals one tenth of one percent, so taxable value times 0.001 times the mills on your statement gives the tax. The state's residential property tax page describes it.

Half of market value counts as assessed value. A building with separate living quarters for fewer than four family units is residential, while apartment buildings of four or more units are commercial. The treasurer's statement lists the actual mills for your district.

The state offers a primary residence credit, and a homestead property tax credit that comes with a renter's refund. Each has eligibility rules on the state tax site. A seller who has claimed one should know the buyer has to qualify separately.

Due dates and penalties

Real estate tax comes due on January 1 after the tax year ends, and the first installment turns delinquent once March 1 passes. The treasurer works from chapter 57-20 of the Century Code.

DateWhat happens
January 1Taxes for the prior tax year become due.
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5 percent discount (paid or postmarked).
March 1First installment is delinquent after this date; a 3 percent penalty applies.
May 1Another 3 percent penalty is added to unpaid first-installment taxes.
July 1Another 3 percent penalty is added.
October 15Second installment is delinquent after this date, with a 6 percent penalty; unpaid first-installment taxes pick up a further 3 percent.

Only general real estate taxes paid in full by February 15 get the discount, and the treasurer applies it ahead of any primary residence credit. Personal property taxes and special assessment installments are excluded. After a weather or other catastrophe emergency declaration, commissioners may add 30 days to the discount period. Mobile homes follow the same discount rule, and statements are printed already reflecting the discount when payment in full comes by February 15.

Not receiving a statement doesn't excuse the bill. The county's property tax page offers payment online by credit card or e-check.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Ward County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Appealing your assessment

Begin at the Tax Equalization office, 225 Third St. SE, Suite 232, Minot 58701, 701-857-6430. When the assessor can't resolve your concern, the path runs through the local board of equalization in April, then the county board, and finally the State Board of Equalization.

Township boards meet the second Monday in April. Minot's City Board of Equalization meets the second Tuesday of April, on a schedule set by the county tax director, and the city contact is 701-857-4108. Meeting dates can move, so verify them yearly.

The state board requires proof under NDCC 57-13-04.3 that you went to the local and county boards first. After that, write to propertytax@nd.gov or call the State Property Tax division at 701-328-3127 to open a state appeal, which involves a questionnaire and supporting evidence.

  • Collect recent comparable sales and any appraisal you have.
  • Take photos of defects the assessor might not know about.
  • Bring the notice and your parcel number to the April meeting.

Winter and flood history

Cold is a real inspection topic. Record lows hit minus 49 degrees Fahrenheit in February and minus 47 in January, which wears on furnaces, pipes and roofs in older houses.

In the 2011 Souris River flood, more than 4,000 Minot homes were flooded and about 11,000 people were evacuated. A buyout program afterward sought to give people with damaged or bought-out homes access to affordable housing. Flood insurance premiums and upcoming FEMA map changes remain live topics. Near the river, buyers will ask about flood zone status and insurance cost. A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can price in that uncertainty, so you don't have to settle it before closing.

What to do before you list

A little homework with the county saves time later. Work through this order.

  1. Find your latest statement and check whether you paid in full by February 15 for the discount, or whether a March 1, May 1 or July 1 penalty has already been added.
  2. Call the treasurer for a payoff figure for the day you expect to close.
  3. If you disagree with the valuation, remember the April board meetings and the sequence from local board to county board to state.
  4. List any special assessments on the parcel, since they get no discount.
  5. Write down any primary residence or homestead credit you've been using, so you and the title company know what changes after the sale.

Owners near the Souris River should also pull their flood repair records, because buyers and insurers often ask for them.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Ward County houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

The tax debt stays on the property, so it's usually paid from your proceeds at closing. Your title company orders a tax search and asks the treasurer for what's owed, including penalties accrued since March 1 or October 15.

Penalties accumulate by date. A summer seller who skipped March 1 would carry the first 3 percent plus the May 1 and July 1 additions. Paying before the next date stops the next penalty, and a payoff quoted for a particular day removes surprises.

  • Request a written payoff from the treasurer or title officer that stays good through your closing date.
  • Look for special assessments, which can't take the 5 percent discount.
  • Find out whether a primary residence or homestead credit you used ends at the sale.

A cash sale uses the same steps without a lender's underwriting, which can delay payoff.

Cash Home Buyers can review a Ward County house with back tax and explain how an as-is offer works, and you owe nothing if you decline. The title company pays the treasurer from your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When is the Ward County property tax discount deadline?

February 15. Pay the year's real estate taxes in full by then, or have the payment postmarked by that date, to receive 5 percent off under NDCC 57-20-09.

Can I pay my Ward County taxes online?

Yes, by credit card or e-check. Look at the county's online payments page before you mail anything.

How do I appeal my Ward County assessment?

Start with the Tax Equalization office, then the township or city board of equalization in April, then the county board. A state appeal is only available after you've applied to the local and county boards.

What is the penalty if I miss March 1?

A 3 percent penalty hits the first installment after March 1, and more 3 percent additions follow on May 1, July 1 and October 15. The second installment carries 6 percent if it's unpaid by October 15.

Can I sell a Ward County house that still has tax due?

Yes. The title company pays the unpaid amount and any penalty from the proceeds at closing, so a cash sale can close on your timeline.

Cass County in brief

Cass County is North Dakota's most populous county, along the Red River on the state's eastern edge. Fargo is the seat and largest city. The 2020 census counted 184,525 residents and the 2025 estimate is 201,794, roughly a quarter of the whole state. Rentals make up a large slice of housing. Nearly half of occupied homes (48.8 percent) were rented at the 2020 count, which means plenty of owners here are landlords. A tenant-occupied house should come with its leases and rent history ready.

Cities, school districts and mill levies

Cass County has 27 incorporated cities, and the city plus the school district decide which mill levy lands on your house. Fargo, West Fargo, Casselton, Kindred, Horace, Mapleton, Hunter, Tower City and Enderlin are among them, along with small places like Alice, Amenia, Ayr and Page. School districts include Fargo Public Schools, West Fargo Public Schools, Kindred, Central Cass, Northern Cass, Maple Valley, Enderlin Area, Hope-Page, May-Port CG and Mapleton, which serves elementary grades only.

A single city can sit in several districts, so one city can have several totals. The county's calculator examples show how much the combination matters:

  • City of Fargo with Fargo School District: 298.43 mills
  • City of Fargo with West Fargo School District: 289.98
  • City of Fargo with Kindred School District: 287.70
  • City of West Fargo: 306.19
  • City of Casselton: 282.41
  • City of Horace with West Fargo School District: 285.88
  • Barnes Township with Fargo School District: 206.74

These are sample totals from the calculator, so compare them against your own statement. A Fargo house in the West Fargo school district carries a lower total than one of equal value in the Fargo district.

Flood history and a sale

The Red River crested at 39.5 feet in 1997 and 40.84 feet in 2009. The Fargo area answered with sandbagging, infrastructure work, buyouts of houses in flood-prone areas and the FM Diversion project. None of this appears on a tax bill, yet it shapes what buyers ask. Be ready to answer three questions honestly:

  • Is the lot in a mapped flood zone, and will the buyer's lender demand flood insurance?
  • Has the basement taken on water, and is there a sump pump or backup system to disclose?
  • Did the city or county buy out nearby lots, and does that change the street?
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Cass County house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Who assesses and who collects

The Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo, ND 58103, houses both offices. Tax Equalization does the valuing and answers at (701) 241-5616. The Finance Office sends bills and takes payment at (701) 241-5600.

Assessed value is half of true and full value. That means market value for homes and commercial property and productivity value for farmland. Taxable value is 9 percent of assessed value for residential property and 10 percent for everything else. The net consolidated tax adds up the taxing bodies' mill levies, multiplies by taxable value and subtracts state-paid property tax relief, which the county ties to N.D.C.C. 57-20-07.1.

The county also runs a property info site at cass.northdakotaassessors.com and an interactive sales app that maps sales near a parcel. Exemptions come in two groups. Discretionary ones include economic expansion and new home construction or remodeling. Non-discretionary ones cover government, school, church and park property. There is also a farm residence exemption, a homestead property tax credit and a disabled veteran credit.

Due dates and penalties

Mailing happens during the first week of December. Half the bill is due March 1 and the rest October 15. Clear the whole amount by February 15 and the consolidated tax shrinks by 5 percent, with specials and drain taxes excluded. If a due date falls on a weekend or county holiday, you have until the next business day.

DatePenalty, first installment and specialsPenalty, second installment
March 13%n/a
May 16%n/a
July 19%n/a
October 1512%6%

Older real estate tax collects 1 percent interest a month, added on the first. You can pay by e-check or card on the web (cards add a convenience fee), at the Finance Office counter, through the mail, or at the secure drop box in front of the Courthouse. The statement lists a permanent parcel number, which changes only if the parcel is split or combined, and a statement number that is reissued annually.

How to appeal your assessment

Cass County describes three stages, beginning with a call to the Tax Equalization office at 701-241-5616 to work things out informally. Next come the boards of equalization:

  1. City board: the first 15 days of April
  2. County board: the first ten days of June
  3. State board: the second Tuesday of August, open only to owners who already appeared before the city and county boards

Missed the boards? A formal abatement remains open. The county wants two copies sent by physical mail, arriving by November 1 of the year following delinquency. The governing law is N.D.C.C. 57-23-04, and the State Tax Commissioner's website hosts the form.

What happens when tax goes delinquent

The Finance Office sends a letter at every stage. Owners with delinquent real estate tax get a Statement of Taxes Owing in March, May, July and October. A Notice of Tax Lien follows in November and explains when interest starts and how foreclosure works. Each May, certified mail carries a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien to parcels delinquent for three years, and a $50 fee is added to those parcels.

Mobile homes take a different path. A Warning and Notice for Delinquent Taxes arrives in August for taxes a year behind, a sheriff's letter comes about ten business days after that, and a sale can eventually be held at the front door of the Courthouse. Penalty details for mobile homes are on the county's collector page.

Selling with taxes owed

The title company pays any unpaid tax from what you receive at closing. Call the Finance Office at (701) 241-5600 and ask for a payoff good through the day you close; the quarterly penalty steps shift the number. Specials and drain taxes are itemized separately and have to be cleared as well.

A simple order of operations helps:

  • Get the payoff in writing and note the date it covers.
  • Write down each special assessment and drain tax line.
  • Give the title company your statement plus the payoff.
  • With tenants in place, add leases and rent records.

Timing matters if you are behind. Statements of Taxes Owing arrive four times a year, and each stage adds cost, so a parcel nearing its third year of delinquency is the one to sell first. A $50 fee and a foreclosure notice land on that parcel in May. Paying at closing from proceeds ends the problem before the county moves further.

We buy Cass County houses as-is, with or without tenants, and we do not quote a price before seeing the property. You owe nothing if you turn our offer down.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay property tax in Cass County?

At the Cass County Finance Office in the Courthouse, 211 9th Street South, Fargo. Online, mail and the drop box outside the Courthouse also work.

How big are Cass County late penalties?

The first installment and specials take 3 percent after March 1, 6 percent on May 1, 9 percent on July 1 and 12 percent on October 15. The second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

Is there an early payment discount?

Yes. Paying the full consolidated tax by February 15 earns 5 percent off, but special assessments and drain taxes do not qualify.

When do the equalization boards meet?

The city board meets in the first 15 days of April and the county board in the first ten days of June. The State Board meets on the second Tuesday of August.

Can I sell with delinquent taxes in Cass County?

Yes. The unpaid tax comes out of your proceeds at closing. Ask the Finance Office at (701) 241-5600 for a payoff figure.

Grand Forks County in brief

Grand Forks County spreads over 1,439 square miles along North Dakota's eastern border, where the Red River marks the line with Minnesota. Its seat and biggest community is the city of Grand Forks. Residents numbered 73,170 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate of 74,501 ranks third in the state.

Beyond Grand Forks itself, the county is made of farm townships and small towns such as Larimore, Northwood and Thompson. Your school district line depends on the parcel's location, since Grand Forks, Thompson, Larimore and Northwood each cover part of the county. East Grand Forks belongs to the same metro area but is across the river in Minnesota, under different state and county rules.

Who handles what

Expect to deal with three county offices. Tax Equalization works with township and city assessors on values. The Treasurer sends bills and takes money. The Recorder files ownership documents. Tax Equalization and the Recorder are both found at 151 South 4th Street, Grand Forks, ND 58201.

  • Tax Equalization Office: uniform assessment, mobile home permits and statements. Call 701-780-8259 (director). Mail to PO Box 5294, Grand Forks ND 58206-5294.
  • County Treasurer: real estate tax bills and payments. Phone 701-780-8292. Write to PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638.
  • Recorder: files deeds and other title documents. Phone 701-780-8262. Write to PO Box 5066.

Who values the parcel depends on where it is. Urban parcels go to the City of Grand Forks Assessing Department. Rural and small town parcels are handled by township and city assessors reporting to the county. Mobile homes are processed by Tax Equalization. Farmland is valued by a separate state method, so check with the office about which category fits yours.

Direct lines also exist for a Real Estate Assessor at 701-780-8245 and a Real Estate Tax Assistant at 701-780-8251. Extensions can change, so confirm when you call.

Due dates and the yearly calendar

The bill is dated January 1 and carries no penalty through March 1. A full-year payment made by February 15 takes 5 percent off. Under state law, statements must be postmarked by December 26. Owners who split the year pay the first installment March 1 and the second October 15.

StepDate
Valuation dateFebruary 1

County board of equalizationFirst 10 days of June
State board of equalizationSecond Tuesday of August
Budget notices from the treasurerAugust 31

5% discount deadlineFebruary 15
Abatement applicationNovember 1 of the next year

Century Code section 57-20-01 adds a 3 percent penalty after March 1, then another on May 1, July 1 and October 15. Second-half payments pick up 6 percent after October 15.

Looking up a parcel online

Several free web tools cover county and city property alike. Vanguard house information pages carry valuation detail. The Tyler iTax site carries real estate and mobile home tax records. An ArcGIS map shows parcel lines, and iDoc holds recorded documents.

  • iTax: today's balance, searched by address, owner name or property number
  • Vanguard: how the parcel was valued
  • iDoc: deeds and other filings, searched by grantor and grantee

Treat the maps as a reference only, since they are no substitute for a legal description. Order a survey or title search if a boundary affects your sale.

How to challenge your assessment

Begin with a conversation with your parcel's assessor. Next comes the local board's April meeting and the county board's June meeting. The state board will lower a value only if you took your appeal through both of those.

A written notice tells each owner the true and full value for this year and last year. Once the August state meeting is over, abatement of the current assessment can still be requested until November 1 of the year after the tax is payable. The State Tax Commissioner's website has the forms.

Owners inside Grand Forks use the city board. For that board, an appeal by letter, phone or electronic message is treated the same as showing up.

When taxes go unpaid

Tax left unpaid turns into a lien on the parcel. When it stays delinquent into a third year, the county can foreclose. Notice is served by June 1, and paying every tax, special, interest charge, penalty and cost by October 1 stops the foreclosure.

Each year the county site publishes its Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien. Once the county holds a tax deed, a former owner can still repurchase ahead of any resale, with the commissioners' approval.

Because the tax lien ranks first, a tax foreclosure can erase a mortgage. Lenders know this, and loan servicers often pay the tax themselves on non-escrow loans and then add that amount to the balance.

Selling with taxes owed

At closing, the unpaid balance comes out of your proceeds, and then the Recorder files the new deed. No deed or mortgage tax exists in North Dakota, so the only cost at that step is a recording fee. For copies, the Recorder charges $1.00 a page, plus $5.00 for the first page of a certified copy.

Inherited the house, or fell behind? Do these things before you list:

  • Ask the Treasurer for the full payoff.
  • Ask the city or township about specials.
  • Search the parcel on iTax to confirm the balance matches your records.
  • Check whether a foreclosure notice has been posted for the parcel.

A cash sale can close without a buyer's lender and appraisal, which removes one cause of delay when a foreclosure date is near. We buy Grand Forks County houses in any condition and coordinate with the title company, so the county balance is paid at closing.

A sale from start to finish

Selling a Grand Forks County house has the same basic order whether you list or take a cash offer. First comes the balance check: the Treasurer's payoff for the real estate tax, and a call to the city or township about any specials. Next the buyer's side orders title work, and any liens show up there. At closing the title company pays the county from your proceeds, you sign the deed, and the Recorder files it.

Two dates can force the pace. One is the February 15 discount deadline, which only matters if you are still the owner when the bill is due. The other is the October 1 foreclosure date for parcels in their third delinquent year. If you are close to either one, say so up front so the buyer and the title company can plan around it.

Bring a few papers to the first conversation: your latest tax statement, any notice from the Treasurer, your mortgage payoff letter if there is a loan, and the deed or estate paperwork if you inherited. With those in hand the title company can usually give you a clear net figure quickly.

What a cash sale skips

A cash buyer does not need a lender's appraisal or loan approval. That removes the waiting period that often delays a closing, and it means the buyer's financing cannot fall through. The house is bought as it stands, so you do not schedule repairs, staging or showings.

The county side does not change. The tax balance, specials and any recorded liens still get paid at closing, and the Recorder still files the deed. What changes is the timeline and how many people have to approve the deal before it closes.

Frequently asked questions

How do I reach the Grand Forks County Treasurer?

Call 701-780-8292 or write to PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638.

Who sets the value of a Grand Forks County home?

Outside city limits, the Tax Equalization Office does so with township and city assessors. Inside Grand Forks, the city's own Assessing Department handles it.

What is the early payment deadline?

February 15. A full-year payment by that day knocks off 5 percent. Otherwise the first half is due March 1.

Where can I see my balance online?

The county's Tyler iTax site searches by address, owner name or property number. Vanguard pages show how the property was valued.

Can a former owner buy a property back after tax foreclosure?

Possibly. State law allows repurchase before the county resells, either in one payment or through an installment contract with the commissioners.
